items.title: Auditory localization and subjective assessment of autonomous cleaning robot sounds: A VR experiment on speed, operating mode and alerting signals
items.abstract: Mobile autonomous robots are increasingly present in everyday environments, where their sounds play a key role in situational awareness and acceptance. Nevertheless, human responses to robot noise remain underexplored. This study examined how robot operating modes and added alerting sounds affect auditory localization and subjective ratings for a professional cleaning robot. Recordings of the robot operating at two velocities during cleaning and non-cleaning were presented. The non-cleaning mode was additionally combined with multi-tone and noise alerting signals, each with and without amplitude modulation. In a VR experiment with within-subjects design, 27 participants performed a localization task and rated annoyance, valence, arousal, and trustworthiness. Localization performance did not differ significantly between sound conditions. Exploratory post hoc analyses indicated that differences between sound conditions varied with participants’ general localization performance, yielding hypotheses for future studies on the role of baseline localization performance. The cleaning sound was rated as most annoying, least pleasant, and least trustworthy, whereas differences between the non-cleaning conditions were rather small. Overall, the alerting signals did not reliably improve localization under the present listening conditions, but some variants may nevertheless warrant further investigation due to their limited negative effects on subjective ratings.

items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
items.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a student model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B student models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

items.title: Automated data to model transformation for constraint programming with AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence for combinatorial optimization depends on high-quality, structured training data, yet transforming ambiguous natural-language descriptions into precise, executable formal models remains a major bottleneck, traditionally requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. We develop CPAM-LLM, an automated constraint-programming modeling framework based on large language models that converts unstructured problem specifications into validated and executable formal models. The framework integrates retrieval-augmented generation grounded in formal concept analysis for structural validation, chaos-mapping-based data augmentation to enhance cross-domain generalization, and dynamic constraint adaptation to accommodate evolving problem settings. We demonstrate its effectiveness across five scenarios, including DNA sequence design, reconfigurable energy storage systems, and unmanned vehicle logistics. The results show that the framework can automate the data-to-model pipeline while adapting reliably to changing requirements, providing a practical approach to automated data formalization and indicating the importance of accessible, high-quality structured data for reliable downstream artificial intelligence applications.

items.title: Autonomy Outpacing Verification: A Stage-Resolved Framework for Measuring How Artificial Intelligence and Automation Are Changing Physics Research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation now operate inside the core loop of physics research. They design optical experiments, shape fusion plasmas, decode quantum errors, select particle collisions in real time and propose new crystals. Existing reviews catalogue these applications by subfield, yet none measures how much decision authority each system holds or how rigorously its outputs are checked. This study introduces two ordinal scales, the Physics Research Autonomy Levels (PRAL, L0 to L5) and the Verification Levels (VL, V0 to V5), and applies them to sixteen documented systems published between 2016 and 2025 in quantum, plasma, particle, gravitational, condensed matter, materials and atmospheric physics. Each system is coded across six research stages: hypothesis, design, execution, analysis, interpretation and reporting. Three results follow. First, autonomy has advanced furthest in execution, where five physics systems act without per-decision human approval, while hypothesis selection and interpretation remain largely human. Second, reported gains concentrate on closed tasks with a fixed objective and a checkable answer, with accelerations from 16 to 2 billion times and equation recovery of 100%, whereas the strongest language model solves 5.7% of open research-level physics challenges. Third, autonomy and verification show no significant association across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.14, p = 0.59). All four systems whose autonomy exceeds their verification by two or more levels act in hypothesis, design or interpretation, while no system confined to execution or analysis shows such a deficit. This difference is defined here as the verification gap. A Verification-Proportional Reporting checklist is proposed that scales evidence requirements with autonomy. The analysis indicates that the binding constraint on AI-driven physics has shifted from computational capability to verification capacity.

items.title: Between Augmentation and Constraint: Digital Technologies Across the Creativity Management Cycle and the Sustainability of Creative Work
items.abstract: Digital technologies, including analytics, algorithmic monitoring and generative artificial intelligence (AI), shape how organisations manage creative work, yet their implications for workplace sustainability remain insufficiently integrated in the existing literature. This perspective develops a process-based creativity management framework through a purposive synthesis of research on creativity, information systems, AI and workplace sustainability. An affordance perspective identifies actor-dependent possibilities for action, while a paradox perspective interprets tensions between augmentation and constraint that may recur across projects. The framework links four managerial functions (planning, organising, motivating and controlling) to digital affordances, tensions and proposed managerial conditions, with generative AI treated as a cross-cutting technology. It distinguishes gains in managerial information from employees’ autonomy, intrinsic motivation and willingness to share tentative ideas, while recognising constraints arising from the organisation of joint ideation. Six testable propositions specify actors and mechanisms at individual and team levels; the sixth links functions across project cycles. The theoretical contribution is to show how function-specific tensions may compound across project cycles and affect the psychological conditions that sustain creative work. Practically, the framework identifies configuration choices for feedback, monitoring, analytics and AI-assisted ideation, distinguishing short-term output gains from the long-term capacity of employees and teams to sustain creativity and well-being.

items.title: Beyond Incrementalism: Navigating Organizational Change, Behavioral Inertia, and Human Fear in AI-Driven Innovation
items.abstract: Organizations now have access to unprecedented compute, generative AI tools, multi-agent workflows, and data analytics capabilities, yet most AI initiatives fail to produce measurable transformation. This paper draws on sixteen transcribed sessions of the Barton College Data Analytics Consortium (October 2025–June 2026), a group of educators and practitioners in higher education, data science consulting, and industrial engineering, read alongside change-management, behavioral, and AI-productivity literature. We argue that the primary bottleneck to AI-driven transformation is neither financial nor technical but organizational: the human behavior that resists change. We identify eight distinct sources of resistance grouped into three families (threat-based, principled, and experiential), describe a “fluency trap” in which polished AI output suppresses scrutiny, and show that data literacy is a frequently missing prerequisite for AI readiness. Case evidence contrasts the automation of existing tasks with genuine agentic redesign of work. We conclude with a three-step framework for adoption (fix the process first, commit to scaling rather than downsizing, and run low-stakes, high-visibility pilots) and argue that without confronting behavioral inertia, organizations do not innovate; they simply produce, in one author’s words, “a digital version of a crappy process.”

items.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

items.title: Caregiver-Informed Safety and System Requirements for Real-Time Feedback During Pediatric Inhaler Use: Qualitative Concept-Elicitation Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Correct use of a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI), usually with a valved holding chamber, depends on use-related conditions that caregivers may not observe directly, including inhalation pattern, actuation-inhalation timing, mask seal, and device orientation. Many digital inhaler systems emphasize actuation or adherence. Systems that infer technique-related conditions from proxy signals may add real-time feedback but also create false reassurance if a positive state is displayed when evidence is inadequate. Caregiver expectations for such feedback and its failure states remain poorly characterized before prototype development. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize caregivers' experiences of pediatric inhaler administration and translate responses to a proposed sensor concept into traceable candidate safety, system, and validation requirements. METHODS: We conducted 23 semistructured concept-elicitation sessions through Zoom videoconference with 27 caregivers of children who currently or previously used a pMDI. Interviews consisted of 19 individual and 4 dyadic sessions pairing 2 caregivers from different households. Sessions were conducted remotely between April and July 2026 from the University of Calgary, Alberta, Canada. Recruitment originated in Calgary and was not geographically restricted. A 6-phase guide examined current practices, difficulties, prior digital-tool use, and responses to a screen-shared clip-on concept incorporating airflow-, timing-, seal-, and orientation-related sensing; on-device feedback; an optional child-facing app; and a caregiver dashboard. No working prototype was evaluated. Approximately 86,000 transcript words underwent hybrid directed and conventional qualitative content analysis using an 18-category codebook. A simple, real-time on-device signal was endorsed by 25 caregivers, but willingness to consider the concept was conditional on reliability (9 caregivers named reasons for abandonment, notably a "false green"), low-friction operation during acute symptoms (12/27), minimal added bulk and technique change, and one or more of clinical validation, clinician recommendation, or a trial pathway (composite category; 23/27). items.title: Caution about AI Generated News Editorial Accountability and Support for Proportionate Regulation in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates the relationship between news credibility and demands for regulation. Caution about substantially AI-generated news need not imply rejection of editorially supervised assistance, while support for accountability need not imply support for unrestricted content controls. This study examines these distinctions in 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records supplied as empirical data from Bangladesh. It analyses five separate statements concerning caution, labelling, accuracy accountability, oversight-related trust and proportionate regulation, with supporting awareness and verification items. Low five-item block reliabilities preclude treating the questionnaire as a validated latent-variable model. Analyses combine response distributions, paired contrasts, joint endorsement patterns, rank correlations and exploratory adjusted logistic regression. Accuracy accountability received 84.2% endorsement and oversight-related trust 83.1%, compared with 69.4% for caution, 68.8% for appropriate labelling and 66.8% for proportionate rules respecting lawful expression. Caution and oversight-related trust were jointly endorsed by 57.7%. Accountability exceeded rules endorsement by 17.4 percentage points, while similar aggregate labelling and rules percentages concealed differing responses in 170 records. No selected correlation or focal binary-model coefficient met the 5% threshold after Holm adjustment. The oversight coefficient was positive but sensitive to response coding and sample restriction. The findings distinguish epistemic caution, editorial responsibility and conditional regulatory support rather than demonstrating a causal trust-to-regulation pathway. They support evaluating particular disclosures and oversight procedures against both informational outcomes and expressive rights. Mixed respondent status, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, single-item measurement and unresolved source-documentation labels constrain generalisation. The contribution is an item-specific account of news governance preferences that does not equate favourable survey responses with verified competence or a mandate for coercive regulation.

items.title: Challenges in using online assessments to measure student understanding in the era of generative AI
items.abstract: Many courses now incorporate online methods for assessing student learning. Some instructors assign questions prior to lecture (e.g., prelecture quizzes) to obtain information that helps them tailor their lessons to the current state of student understanding. To assess curriculum efficacy, physics education researchers often use “pretests,” inventories, etc. that provide baseline data that can be compared to results from post-tests. These assessments were initially given on paper but moved online in the early 2000s. At the University of Washington, we found that the impact of this change was minimal; the results of our pretests stayed essentially the same when given on paper or online and were consistent from quarter to quarter and instructor to instructor. However, we have begun to observe systematic changes in pretest performance that are consistent with students using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to answer pretests, even though they are scored only on effort, not correctness. Using two-proportion z -tests, mixed-effects logistic regression, and Welch’s t tests to analyze response length of explanations, this paper documents the nature and extent of these changes across 39 questions in two introductory algebra-based physics courses. This paper presents results that suggest caution to those using online quizzes to probe student understanding—both before and/or after instruction. We have seen increases in correct responses on pretests as great as 36%, but we have also seen significant decreases on questions that AI tools have tended to answer incorrectly. These findings raise important questions about the validity of online assessments and are intended to raise awareness for anyone using online tests to assess student learning. It remains an open question as to whether, and how, AI can be leveraged to improve instruction.

items.title: Changes in Psychological Well-being and Homesickness Following a Twelve Day Generative AI Assisted Activity Program among Pakistani International Students in China
items.abstract: International students’ psychological adjustment is shaped by challenges involving everyday agency, social connection, and separation from familiar support networks. This study examined short-term changes in psychological wellbeing, social self-efficacy, and homesickness following a 12-day generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted daily activity programme among Pakistani international students in China. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the programme combined activities intended to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness with GenAI-assisted planning, reflection, and conversational rehearsal. Twenty-eight participants completed self-report assessments immediately before and after the programme in a single-group pre-test–post-test design. Outcomes were assessed using Ryff’s Psychological Well-Being Scale, a social self-efficacy measure, and the homesickness subscale of the Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students. Reported Wilcoxon signed-rank analyses indicated an increase in overall psychological wellbeing from 86.38 to 98.14 (p = .004) and a decrease in homesickness from 10.90 to 7.52 (p = .002). Social self-efficacy increased from 96.38 to 107.34, although this change was not statistically significant (p = .092). These findings provide preliminary evidence of favourable changes in selected psychosocial outcomes during participation in a structured GenAI-assisted activity programme. However, the absence of a comparison group, the small purposively recruited sample, and the lack of follow-up prevent attribution of these changes to GenAI or conclusions about their durability. The study offers an initial application of need-supportive programme design in a South–South educational mobility context and provides a basis for subsequent controlled evaluation.

items.title: Cognitive and attitudinal correlates of trust in AI-generated content among university students in Türkiye
items.abstract: We examined cognitive and attitudinal correlates of trust in AI-generated content in a 2025 cross-sectional survey in Türkiye. The respondent cohort comprised 232 records; 207 self-identified generative AI users completed the focal measures. A hierarchical regression distinguished perceived Generative AI Literacy, behavioral use frequency, positive and negative AI attitudes, an exploratory post-truth index, and risk/regulatory concern. Literacy and frequency explained 0.2% of trust variance; attitudes added 12.2%, and the joint post-truth/concern block added 13.6%. The final model explained 26.0% (adjusted R² = 0.238). Positive attitude (β = 0.310), negative attitude (β = −0.215), and the post-truth index (β = 0.425) had significant conditional associations. Negative attitude had an essentially null zero-order association ( r = .021). The post-truth index uniquely accounted for 13.4% points beyond the other measured predictors. Exploratory structure analyses supported a dominant common dimension but also revealed residual item clustering; content-domain sensitivity analyses localized the association mainly to devaluation of factual truth. Education-group differences did not survive adjustment across six outcome tests. These self-report associations do not establish causality, objective misinformation susceptibility, or a validated unitary post-truth disposition.

items.title: Cognitive and Organisational Dynamics of Decision-Making in Urban Flood Emergencies for Sustainable and Resilient Cities: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Urban flood events are increasing in frequency and severity, threatening the social, economic and environmental sustainability of cities and placing considerable strain on decision-makers operating in complex and high-pressure environments. While the technical and infrastructural aspects of flood response have been widely examined, systematic attention to the psychological and organisational dimensions of decision-making during flood emergencies remains limited. This study synthesises the existing literature on how cognitive, psychological, institutional, technological, and social factors influence decision-making under pressure in urban flood contexts. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines to ensure a transparent, rigorous, and reproducible study-selection process. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2009 and 2026 were retrieved from the Scopus database and screened against predefined eligibility criteria. The search initially identified 376 records. After removing 5 duplicates, 371 records underwent title and abstract screening, of which 8 were excluded. The remaining 363 articles were assessed for full-text eligibility, resulting in the exclusion of 133 articles and the inclusion of 230 studies in the final synthesis. Thematic analysis was employed to identify key decision-making variables, which were subsequently modelled using Vensim to map causal relationships and feedback mechanisms among cognitive stressors, organisational conditions, technological factors, and decision quality. The findings reveal that communication breakdowns can amplify role ambiguity and diminish situational awareness, creating reinforcing cycles that undermine decision quality. Stress-induced cognitive limitations and institutional fragmentation also emerged as important influences on response effectiveness. Overall, urban flood emergency decision-making is shaped by interconnected relationships among cognitive load, time pressure, leadership clarity, institutional coordination, technological support, and organisational structures. By integrating behavioural, organisational, technological, and social dimensions, this study provides a systems-based understanding of urban flood emergency decision-making and identifies critical intervention points for strengthening real-time response effectiveness. Because the quality of emergency decisions determines whether lives, livelihoods, infrastructure and ecosystem services are protected, and whether these protections are distributed equitably, the findings position flood emergency decision-making as a core component of sustainable urban development and support progress towards Sustainable Development Goals 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and 13 (Climate Action) and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.

items.title: Cognitive workload-guided learning of manipulation behaviors from human demonstrations in industrial settings
items.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has emerged as a promising paradigm in robotics. Especially in the context of disassembly tasks in circular factories, this would allow factory workers to teach robotics new skills without the need for robotics engineers or programmers, thus enabling flexible and scalable automation in modern manufacturing systems. However, collecting demonstrations only as a pre-deployment step is not flexible enough for rapidly changing production contexts. In circular manufacturing, end-of-life conditions are revealed during processing, and even in high-mix conventional manufacturing, variants and edge cases evolve faster than static offline datasets. We therefore argue for an integrated train-while-operate approach in which demonstrations are collected during productive operation, and policies are continuously updated. A key challenge of this approach is fluctuating demonstration quality caused by varying operator cognitive workload under real factory demands. This paper addresses this problem with a cognitive-workload-guided dataset-filtering framework for industrial learning from demonstration. We estimate demonstrator cognitive and physical workload during task execution and filter demonstrations collected under elevated workload. The framework is implemented and evaluated in a robot teleoperation scenario where cognitive workload is systematically varied to emulate realistic workload fluctuations and estimated using two sensing systems for comparison. Experimental results show that filtering the dataset with the proposed heuristics improves the performance of the learned motion models.

items.title: Competition Shapes Students’ Use of Generative AI in Creative Problem-Solving: Behavioral Distancing and Its Individual and Collective Changes
items.abstract: Generative AI can support students' learning and problem-solving, yet little is known about whether and how human-AI collaboration changes across social contexts. This study introduces competition as an important social context and examines how it shapes students' use of AI-generated content in creative problem-solving. A total of 92 undergraduates were randomly assigned to competition or no-competition conditions and completed three creative problem-solving tasks with GenAI support, yielding 276 student-task observations. Semantic similarity analysis, behavioral coding, regression analysis, and permutation tests were used to examine changes in AI-content use and their individual- and collective-level changes. Results showed that competition reduced students' semantic overlap with AI-generated content and increased almost full rejection of AI suggestions, without a corresponding statistically detectable increase in self-directed improvement. Competition was associated with greater idea fluency and flexibility, but lower fluency-normalized flexibility, and neither individual semantic distinctiveness nor collective semantic diversity consistently increased. Together, these findings distinguish behavioral distancing from constructive human agency in AI-supported problem-solving: using less AI-generated content does not necessarily mean engaging with AI more independently or achieving greater relative diversity. The study therefore highlights human-AI collaboration as a socially situated process and shifts attention from the amount of AI use to the performance of students' engagement with AI-generated content. Supporting effective AI-assisted learning may require fostering students' capacity to critically evaluate, transform, and extend AI-generated ideas rather than simply encouraging greater or lesser reliance on GenAI.

items.title: Connection Without Presence: AI & the “Death of Man”
items.abstract: This essay takes its point of departure from a short story by the American novelist Laura van den Berg. It argues that van den Berg’s “Samatha” can be read as a “post-speculative realist” allegory for our relationship with emerging AI technologies. In particular, it is concerned with analyzing how the widespread adoption of large language model chatbots is transforming our relationships with ourselves and others. It attempts to describe this experience in terms of a structure that I call “connection without presence.” Connection without presence is an attempt to name the strange, posthuman form of desire that is at work in our relationship with many communications technologies. In terms of the Foucaultian philosophy, it suggests that the chatbot is a confessional wherein the human being whispers their desire to disappear-and learns to enjoy its submission.

items.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
items.abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

items.title: Deliberation Within AI: A Reproducible Pipeline for Multi-Agent Deliberation Simulation
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have renewed interest in whether large language models can simulate aspects of public deliberation. Current deliberation simulations remain methodologically fragile: fluent conversational outputs are often treated as evidence of deliberative quality despite limited reproducibility, weak safeguards for viewpoint diversity, and limited systematic evaluation. This article argues that AI-deliberation simulations can function as credible analytical instruments only if they incorporate infrastructures for reproducibility, plurality preservation, and deliberative quality assessment. The article develops a stage-structured method for deliberative simulation combining persona validation, plurality auditing, and discourse-quality assessment within a reproducible pipeline. The framework is presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and evaluated through a simulation study on the June 2023 Swiss federal referendum on the Climate and Innovation Act together with a batch replication study comparing direct and structured deliberation architectures. The findings show that, as an integrated theory-driven architecture, the structured pipeline generates more stable deliberative dynamics than unconstrained interaction, including clearer plurality preservation and more coherent opinion updating. At the same time, the simulations remain below human minipublics in terms of contextual grounding and justificatory depth. The article positions AI-deliberation simulations as methodological infrastructures for cumulative and empirically testable research on AI-supported deliberation in digital governance.

items.title: Designing Digital Learning Environments Through Cognitive Load Theory and Universal Design for Learning: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Digital learning environments require pedagogical approaches that address students’ cognitive demands and variability. This scoping review maps how Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) inform the design of digital learning environments across educational contexts, examining design principles, implementation characteristics, research methods, and reported outcomes. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC. Eligibility criteria focused on empirical journal articles published in English that described, analysed, or evaluated digital environments designed using principles of CLT and/or UDL. Data were organised into a matrix covering study characteristics, theoretical frameworks, design elements, assessment instruments, and findings. The review included 34 studies: 17 were classified as CLT-oriented, 16 as UDL-oriented, and one explicitly combined both frameworks. The environments analysed included learning management systems, MOOCs, multimedia resources, mobile applications, immersive environments, and educational games. CLT-oriented designs emphasised segmentation, cueing, worked examples, and cognitive load management; in contrast, UDL-oriented designs highlighted accessible resources, flexible participation, and multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. Reported outcomes included academic performance, cognitive load, engagement, motivation, accessibility, and usability. Heterogeneity in research designs and assessment measures limits conclusions regarding comparative effectiveness. The mapping identifies limited explicit integration of CLT and UDL and highlights the need for further research into their operational alignment in digital instructional design.

items.title: Designing engagement in artificial intelligence education: algorithmic citizenship, agency and authentic tasks
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered pupils’ daily lives before it has been incorporated into school curricula, yet schools tend to view it either as a risk to be contained or as a productivity tool to be mastered, neglecting pupils’ ability to understand, question and transform the algorithmic systems that shape their experience. This theoretical contribution proposes a conceptual foundation for an engaging AI education, in which algorithmic citizenship is practised through authentic tasks rather than taught as content. The study conducts a critical, integrative literature review that brings together research on school engagement, self-determination theory, authentic learning, AI literacy, and critical data studies, and reinterprets the criteria for authentic learning in light of the distinctive characteristics of algorithmic objects: opacity, mutability, reflexivity, and distributed effects. The analysis identifies three shifts in the classical criteria (from relevance to the real world to relevance to the lived world; from a multiplicity of perspectives to political plurality; and from integrated assessment to intervention) and a framework of design principles structured across three levels, relating to motivational needs, scaffolding and persistence, illustrated by three task scenarios. The paper argues that strong engagement arises when students recognise that the task concerns them and that their own actions can influence it, and it outlines its limitations, ethical issues and hypotheses for empirical research.

items.title: Designing Social Stories™ with GenAI. A Dialogic environment supporting the Individualized Education Plan
items.abstract: Writing a Social Story requires information about the learner and the situation, together with attention to language and accuracy. Generative artificial intelligence may assist with drafting, but its output requires review before educational use. This paper describes a Social Stories™ generation tool developed within the Socrate platform at the University of Salerno as part of a project supporting Individualized Education Plan design. The tool combines a module for collecting educational information with a technical module for configuring generation and review. Users specify the learner’s communication profile, the context, the story’s purpose and available support. A Python backend coordinates language model generation, automated checks and revision, with separate drafting and reviewing roles. The procedures are designed to identify structural problems, unsupported assumptions and coercive or judgmental wording. Teachers retain responsibility for checking the narrative and deciding whether it is appropriate for the learner. Feedback and revision records provide material for professional discussion and training. The paper outlines the tool’s architecture and the evaluation needed to assess narrative quality and educational use. Future work will compare local and general-purpose models through expert assessment and examine whether stories support learners’ understanding in the situations for which they are written.

items.title: Developing and validating the Chinese version of the Perceived Trustworthiness of Large Language Models Scale (PT-LLM-8)
items.abstract: The trustworthiness of technology constitutes a critical determinant of user adoption, particularly regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life. Currently, prominent AI products rely on large language models (LLMs), and such LLMs assist users in personal and professional contexts. To systematically investigate the perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, we provide a psychometrically sound measurement instrument for assessing perceived trustworthiness of LLMs. Given the importance of the Chinese market for current AI developments, the present study examined the psychometric properties of a Chinese version of the Perceived Trustworthiness of Large Language Models Scale (PT-LLM-8) [1] and its association with Big Five personality traits, self-efficacy, and self-esteem. Based on the responses of 478 Chinese adults, the Chinese PT-LLM-8 showed good psychometric properties, including strong internal consistency and a clear unidimensional factor structure. Evidence of construct validity was provided by theoretically expected associations between PT-LLM-8 score and self-efficacy, self-esteem, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. These findings provide psychometric support for the Chinese version of the PT-LLM-8 as a measure of perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, consistent with the cumulative cross-linguistic evidence for the instrument across its English [1], German [2] and Chinese versions.

items.title: Development of a Virtual Reality Learning Environment for Computer Assembly Competency in Pre-Service Teachers Using Generative AI-Produced Media
items.abstract: Thai computer teacher trainees must assemble and repair computers during their practicum, yet many get little hands-on practice because laboratory machines are scarce, outdated, and easily damaged. This design-and-development study built a virtual reality learning environment (VRLE) for computer assembly on a Meta Quest 3 headset, with controller-free hand tracking, three simulation rooms mapped to a national occupational competency unit, and learning media produced with generative AI. Development followed the ADDIE model, and a feasibility tryout used a one-group pretest–posttest design. Three content experts and three technical experts rated content (M = 4.74) and technical quality (M = 4.45) as very good, with interaction and usability the weakest domain (M = 4.11). Among 35 pre-service teachers with matched tests, achievement rose from 8.20 to 9.09 out of 10 (Wilcoxon z = 2.95, p = .002, r = .50; t(34) = 2.92, dz = 0.49). After a sequence of website lessons, VR practice, real-hardware practice, and debriefing, mean competency on real hardware was 4.85 (n = 36) and mean satisfaction was 4.79 (n = 28), both with ceiling effects. Without a control group, the results show that the VRLE is feasible and well received, not that it caused the gains.

items.title: Didactic orchestration integrating artificial intelligence tools to develop creative thinking skills in students
items.abstract: Introduction This study examined changes in students' self-reported creativity-related behaviors following an educational intervention combining artificial intelligence (AI) tools and the DRAE instructional model (Diagnosis, Recreation, Application, and Estimation). Methods A one-group preexperimental pretest-posttest questionnaire design was complemented by semi-structured interviews and direct-observation records. The quantitative analysis included 551 valid paired EvaCreIA records, exceeding the minimum sample target of 543. The questionnaire assessed Generate Diverse Ideas (GID), Generate Creative Ideas (GIC), and Evaluate and Improve Ideas (EMI). Complementary interview indicators were calculated from 703 eligible pretest and 730 eligible posttest records, while direct observation included 568 completed checklist records. Results Posttest means exceeded pretest means by 0.222, 0.270, and 0.241 points for GID, GIC, and EMI, respectively, on a five-point scale. Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment ( p < .001). Rank-biserial correlations were 0.340 for GID, 0.387 for GIC, 0.340 for EMI, and 0.374 for the supplementary overall score. The complementary interview indicators showed higher favorable-response percentages at posttest. Discussion The results indicate changes in self-reported creativity-related behaviors following the combined educational intervention. However, retrospective record linkage, limitations in cross-instrument correspondence, self-report measurement, and the absence of a comparison group restrict causal interpretation. The findings do not establish an independent causal effect of AI or validate the DRAE model.

items.title: Digital affordances for customer engagement: The role of co-creation climate, social media manager’s characteristics, and creative brand content
items.abstract: Although firms increasingly rely on social media to reach, high platform activity does not automatically yield user engagement and can suppress participation when communication strategies are misaligned. This underscores a central IS challenge: understanding how organizations can mobilize platform affordances to craft content that captures attention and stimulates interaction. Moreover, despite the importance of creativity for innovation and digital transformation, IS research has devoted limited attention to it, especially from a market perspective. As a result, we know relatively little about how organizational practices and managerial capabilities align with platform affordances to foster market-facing perceptions of creativity and, ultimately, customer-contributed value. Addressing these gaps, this study investigates how micro-level managerial capabilities and organizational routines relate to follower-perceived content creativity and multidimensional customer engagement. Utilizing multi-source, dyadic and triadic data from two empirical studies in Spain, we test a multilevel sociotechnical model using structural equation modeling. The findings indicate that organizational co-creation practices, as well as social media managers' task adaptivity and emotional intelligence, are positively associated with content originality and relevance through the enactment of platform affordances. Furthermore, follower-perceived content creativity is positively associated with second-order customer engagement, with market competitive intensity conditioning these pathways. The study advances affordance theory by extending its analytical scope from internal enterprise systems to open digital platforms, while conceptualizing digital creativity as an externally evaluated artifact. Practically, the results suggest that firms cannot rely on raw connectivity alone; managers and organizations must actively orchestrate adaptive iteration and collaborative listening to foster customer-contributed value.

items.title: Dynamic Human-Robot Role Allocation through Entropy-Based Monitoring and LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Role allocation strategies in human-robot collaboration typically assign tasks to both the human and the robot, limiting the user's ability to take initiative. Furthermore, allocation decisions may conflict with the user's intentions, and the rationale behind such allocations may remain unclear, potentially reducing both acceptance and collaboration fluency. The novelty of the proposed framework is that the human is left free to contribute to the task, while the robot is dynamically allocated activities through a cost-driven Behavior Tree architecture according to user-expressed preferences and behavior. Explicit preferences are extracted from natural language instructions using a large language model, whereas human activity is monitored online through a Shannon entropy-based analysis of hand-object interactions. Furthermore, the framework can recognize anomalies in human execution and autonomously trigger corrective robot actions. The approach was validated through a pilot study and a multi-subject experiment involving 14 participants. Results demonstrate the potential of such an allocation strategy for enabling intuitive and engaging collaboration without increasing the perceived workload.

items.title: EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT IN NIGERIA: CHALLENGES FOR DIGITAL LEARNING SYSTEMS
items.abstract: The emergence of digital technologies, without doubt has continued to reshape educational systems across the globe, creating new opportunities for sustainable development in developing countries such as Nigeria. This study examines the nexus between emerging technologies and sustainable development with particular emphasis on digital learning systems in Nigeria. The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, virtual learning platforms, mobile technologies, and digital communication tools has significantly transformed teaching, learning and knowledge dissemination in educational institutions. Despite these advancements, challenges such as inadequate technological infrastructure, poor internet connectivity, digital inequality, limited technical skills and inconsistent policy implementation has continued to undermine the effectiveness of digital learning systems in Nigeria. The paper adopts qualitative approach and makes use of secondary sources of data to bridge the gap in knowledge. The study examines the role of emerging technologies in promoting sustainable digital learning systems in Nigeria, identify the challenges associated with the adoption of digital learning technologies in educational institutions; and investigate the challenges affecting the effective integration of emerging technologies into Nigeria's educational system. The paper hinges on the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovation Theory as its theoretical frameworks. While Technology Acceptance Model explains users' acceptance and utilization of digital technologies based on perceived usefulness and ease of use. The diffusion of Innovation Theory provides insight into how technological innovations spread are adopted within educational and social systems. The paper concludes that although emerging technologies possess significant potential for transforming Nigeria's educational landscape and advancing sustainable development, deliberate investments in infrastructure, digital literacy, and supportive policies are necessary for achieving long-term effectiveness and inclusiveness

items.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
items.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

items.title: Ethical considerations in AI-enabled electrocardiography: a narrative review
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled electrocardiography (ECG) can detect arrhythmias, structural abnormalities, and physiological patterns not readily apparent through conventional interpretation. However, its rapid clinical integration raises ethical concerns. This review critically synthesizes literature on bias and fairness, privacy and confidentiality, explainability and transparency, clinical trust and automation bias, and governance and accountability. Methods We conducted a narrative review using structured searches of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. Review preparation was informed by the SANRA quality-assessment scale, and study selection was summarized using a flow diagram adapted from PRISMA-ScR (435 records identified; 46 studies included). Studies were eligible if they substantively examined ethical considerations in AI-ECG; those addressing technical performance alone were excluded. Evidence was classified by study design and clinical maturity. Results Ethical risks arose throughout the AI-ECG lifecycle, beyond the algorithm itself. Studies documented performance disparities across sex, age, race, and ethnicity, alongside vulnerabilities involving membership inference, biometric re-identification, and unintended attribute inference. Explainability remained inadequately evaluated, while automation bias raised concerns about clinical decision-making and patient safety. Governance and post-deployment oversight remained fragmented. Most quantitative evidence came from retrospective or experimental proof-of-concept studies rather than externally validated or clinically deployed systems. Discussion Responsible AI-ECG implementation requires a lifecycle approach addressing upstream bias, privacy safeguards, clinically meaningful explanations, clinician oversight, and post-deployment surveillance. We propose Inherent Protocol Bias (IPB) as an organizing framework linking downstream ethical risks to decisions in study design, data collection, validation, and deployment. Unlike dataset bias, selection bias, spectrum bias, measurement bias, and cohort-origin confounding, which describe specific sources or manifestations of error, IPB emphasizes the protocol-level decisions through which established biases arise or persist. IPB is not a new statistical form of bias but a framework for identifying actionable intervention points. We outline potential applications for improving fairness, privacy, accountability, and clinical trust; however, these recommendations remain conceptual and require empirical evaluation.

items.title: Ethical Dilemmas of AI Use in PAI Learning: A Teacher's Perception and Grade X Students' Learning Behaviors at MA As Syakur
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) offers opportunities to enhance students’ understanding but also raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty and the accuracy of religious information. This study aims to analyze AI use, teacher perceptions, students’ learning behaviors, and the ethical dilemmas arising at MA As Syakur. Employing a descriptive qualitative approach, the study involved one IRE teacher and eight Grade X students selected purposively. Data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of 33 student assignment books, then analyzed thematically. The findings reveal five patterns of AI use, ranging from seeking explanations and comparing information to directly copying AI-generated answers. Four of the eight student informants were found to have copied AI-generated answers into their assignment books. The teacher demonstrated an open yet cautious attitude, emphasizing the importance of guidance and information verification. This study highlights the need to promote AI literacy, academic honesty, and Islamic ethical values, particularly amanah (trustworthiness) and tabayyun (careful verification), in IRE learning. Future research should involve more madrasahs and employ longitudinal observations.

items.title: Ethical Dimensions of Computational Social Science Research: A Primer
items.abstract: This primer discusses the ethical questions raised by computational social science (CSS), that is, research that analyses data generated at scale by digital platforms, networked devices, and public administrations. Much of the ethical guidance available to CSS researchers was developed for clinical and interventional research, and it assumes a bounded study, an identifiable participant, and an occasion on which consent can be sought. Since much CSS research lacks these features, the primer examines where this guidance fits and where it does not. The primer is organised around six themes: data, privacy, and power; bias and equity; conceptual clarity and value-laden choices; stakeholder impact, justice, and participatory research; ethical communication and public engagement; and the use of generative AI in the research process. Each theme is introduced conceptually, illustrated with cases from the published literature, and followed by reflection questions that researchers can ask of their own projects. The primer is intended for researchers, research ethics committees, and teaching. It pays particular attention to research on administrative registers, including data held by Statistics Netherlands. The research for this publication was partly funded by ODISSEI, the Dutch national research infrastructure for the social sciences.

items.title: Evaluation of vibration transmissibility and ergonomic usability of anti-vibration gloves at real workstations
items.abstract: Exposure to hand transmitted vibration is common in workplaces using hand held-tools and contributes to upper limb disorders, including hand-arm vibration syndrome. Anti-vibration gloves are often the only personal protective equipment available, but their use remains limited because of discomfort and reduced manual dexterity, so glove assessment should extend beyond laboratory testing to real working conditions. This article proposes an extension of ISO 10819 based on eight vibration transmission coefficients determined in situ, together with comfort-related parameters such as dexterity and the force required to bend the fingers. The method was applied at four workstations differing in vibration characteristics, using an ISO 10819-compliant glove of a new design as a case study. Frequency-weighted exposure was reduced by 10-56% depending on the workstation, although at one workstation the results indicated amplification in one of the analysed axes. Compliance with ISO 10819 therefore does not guarantee protection at every workstation.

items.title: Evidence-Grounded Hybrid Agentic AI for Trustworthy AI Risk Communication Assessment in SEC Form 10-K Disclosures
items.abstract: Public companies increasingly communicate risks related to artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, automation, algorithmic decision-making, data privacy, security, bias, and regulatory uncertainty in annual risk-factor disclosures. However, assessing whether these AI-risk and trustworthy-AI communication claims are specific, evidence-grounded, or largely boilerplate remains difficult because Form 10-K Item 1A disclosures combine forward-looking risk language, legal disclaimers, product descriptions, governance statements, and uncertain regulatory developments. This study develops an evidence-grounded hybrid agentic AI framework for assessing AI risk communication in SEC Form 10-K disclosures. The task is framed as textual support assessment rather than an independent determination of a company's actual AI risk exposure, legal compliance, product safety, or trustworthiness. Using a corpus of 160 Form 10-K filings collected from SEC EDGAR, we identify 101 filings with AI-related Item 1A risk-factor language and construct an 80-claim manually annotated gold sample across 48 companies. We compare five approaches: a transparent rule-based baseline, a TF-IDF retrieval baseline, a single-prompt large language model (LLM) baseline, a pure multi-agent reasoning baseline, and the proposed hybrid agentic adjudication method. The hybrid method achieves the strongest performance on trustworthiness-dimension classification and evidence-support assessment, with 0.725 dimension accuracy, 0.667 dimension macro-F1, 0.750 support accuracy, and 0.734 support macro-F1. We further add an explainability and auditability analysis using claim-level audit traces and a SHAP-based structured-feature surrogate for supported versus non-supported evidence labels. The findings suggest that evidence-grounded hybrid agentic AI can support auditable analysis of trustworthy-AI risk communication, while also showing that direct LLM prompting can be poorly calibrated for evidence-support judgments.

items.title: Executive function and task engagement in workload and mental fatigue: a multi-domain study using a novel adaptive paradigm
items.abstract: This experimental study investigated how perceived workload is influenced by executive function load (lower, higher) and task engagement (via non-adaptive or adaptive task pacing), across the three domains of inhibition, switching, and updating. It further explored how mental fatigue develops from sustained performance under varying levels of these factors. Seventy-two adults were randomly allocated to three groups, each completing six tasks at an individualised pace and in a distinct combination of executive function load and task engagement. Workload was not altered by executive function load, but it increased significantly under adaptive pacing, with the most pronounced effect in the inhibition domain. Mental fatigue emerged across all conditions regardless of workload differences, but its onset was anticipated under low executive function load with non-adaptive pacing and under high executive function load with adaptive pacing. These findings suggest that under- and over-stimulation may be two different paths to mental fatigue.

items.title: Explainable AI for Streaming Process Mining: Overview, Challenges and Outlook
items.abstract: Streaming Process Mining (SPM) enables the real-time analysis of business processes through the continuous processing of event streams, providing timely insights and facilitating quick decisions. Although SPM supports various applications in multiple domain areas, it often relies on data-driven algorithms that lack interpretability, limiting user acceptance and trust. To tackle such shortcomings, explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) offers promising techniques to improve transparency and understanding of the applied approach. Despite their complementarity, SPM and XAI originate from distinct research communities, each with its own focus, methodologies, and evaluation criteria. This paper provides an overview of the intersection between XAI and SPM. We categorize existing work according to the SPM tasks addressed, the XAI methodologies used, and the level of interpretability from the end-user’s perspective. In addition, we identify key research challenges and propose future directions aimed at developing more human-centered and trustworthy SPM approaches. Our findings emphasize the importance of aligning algorithmic performance and human comprehension to support responsible decision making in dynamic process environments.

items.title: Exploring EFL students’ critical AI literacy in generative AI-assisted essay revision: insights into profiles and trajectories
items.abstract: This study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) students demonstrate and develop Critical AI Literacy (CAIL) in generative AI-assisted essay revision. Drawing on the APSE model, which conceptualizes CAIL across four dimensions (awareness, positionality, interaction strategies, and evaluation), we conducted a longitudinal case study of three focal students across four writing tasks throughout a semester. Data sources included student-AI interaction logs, think-aloud protocols, stimulated recall interviews, and both initial and revised essay drafts. Qualitative analyses were conducted to trace patterns and changes in students’ CAIL. Findings show that all three students demonstrated CAIL across the four dimensions, although critical evaluation and critical positionality emerged as the most salient dimensions. Students selectively integrated AI feedback based on rhetorical fit, linguistic appropriateness, and factual accuracy, demonstrating various levels of agency. Over time, two students became increasingly selective and context-sensitive in their engagement with AI, whereas the third demonstrated strategic engagement from the outset but showed substantial task-to-task variation in feedback uptake. Overall, the students’ trajectories were heterogeneous and task-dependent rather than uniformly progressive. These patterns challenge linear models of AI literacy and highlight its situated nature in EFL writing contexts. Pedagogically, the study calls for differentiated instruction that fosters evaluative judgment and self-representation alongside prompt design. The findings contribute to a growing body of research advocating for more nuanced, learner-centered approaches to AI integration in foreign language writing.

items.title: Eye and Face Protection Violations Have Ranked Among OSHA’s Top 10 Since 2018: An Evidence-Based Framework for Intelligent Detection, Risk Assessment, and Timely Intervention
items.abstract: Eye and face protection violations under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard have repeatedly appeared among the most frequently cited federal workplace safety standards since fiscal year 2018, highlighting persistent challenges in personal protective equipment (PPE) compliance, hazard recognition, and occupational safety management. Workers in construction, manufacturing, and other high-risk industrial environments remain vulnerable to eye and facial injuries arising from flying particles, chemical splashes, molten materials, dust, and other hazardous exposures. Although conventional workplace inspections, safety training, and supervisory monitoring remain essential, these approaches are often constrained by limited observation coverage, intermittent assessments, delayed identification of violations, and inconsistent enforcement. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and edge computing offer opportunities to strengthen PPE monitoring through automated recognition, contextual risk assessment, and timely corrective intervention. This study examines the regulatory, technological, and operational challenges associated with persistent eye and face protection violations and develops an evidence-based framework for integrating AI-assisted PPE detection with proactive occupational safety management. Specifically, it investigates how deep learning-based object detection, worker–PPE association, pose estimation, edge inference, hazard-aware decision rules, and human-centered intervention mechanisms can improve the identification, prioritization, and resolution of potentially unsafe PPE practices. An evidence-based narrative synthesis was conducted using OSHA regulatory information and peer-reviewed literature addressing occupational eye and face injuries, PPE compliance monitoring, computer vision architectures, machine learning, workplace hazard assessment, and safety management systems. Particular attention was given to You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detection models, pose and key point estimation, lightweight edge-computing architectures, temporal tracking, and multiclass PPE classification. Existing studies were critically examined to identify methodological strengths, operational limitations, performance variability, and research gaps. Building on the reviewed evidence, this study develops a risk-informed occupational eye and face protection assessment methodology that integrates regulatory requirements, hazard exposure, protective equipment adequacy, monitoring reliability, and corrective intervention effectiveness. Rather than proposing another automated PPE detection architecture, the methodology examines how technology-generated observations can be interpreted within task-specific safety requirements and translated into measurable intervention priorities. It distinguishes confirmed equipment absence, incorrect positioning, unsuitable protection, and insufficient visual evidence while incorporating mathematical indicators for hazard-weighted prioritization, detection reliability, corrective-action timeliness, and occupational injury incidence. Computer vision and edge-based monitoring are examined as supporting sources of safety evidence rather than independent injury-prevention solutions. The resulting methodology provides a structured basis for prospective evaluation of monitoring-supported safety interventions. No newly trained detection model, experimental dataset, or completed field trial is reported. Unlike conventional PPE recognition systems that primarily identify equipment presence, the framework emphasizes whether appropriate protective equipment is correctly positioned, associated with the exposed worker, and suitable for the prevailing occupational hazard. It also incorporates human oversight, privacy safeguards, explainable decision support, and mechanisms for managing false-positive detections and ambiguous visual conditions. The study proposes a multidimensional evaluation strategy extending beyond conventional computer vision metrics such as precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed. Recommended performance indicators include event-level violation detection sensitivity, false alerts per worker-hour, end-to-end notification latency, time to verified corrective action, unresolved hazardous exposure duration, recurrence of PPE violations, and longitudinal occupational injury outcomes. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for comparing AI-assisted monitoring with conventional safety inspection approaches while distinguishing technical detection performance from operational intervention effectiveness. It further identifies research priorities involving small-object recognition, transparent protective eyewear detection, cross-site generalizability, risk-based alert optimization, worker privacy, and prospective validation of injury-prevention outcomes. AI-assisted eye and face protection monitoring represents a promising approach to addressing persistent PPE compliance challenges through continuous observation, contextual violation assessment, and timely intervention. However, high detection accuracy and rapid alert generation alone do not demonstrate reductions in occupational injuries. Effective prevention requires reliable worker - PPE association, hazard-specific compliance assessment, accountable human intervention, verified corrective action, and integration with established occupational safety procedures. The proposed framework advances the conceptual foundation for transforming automated PPE recognition into a measurable, human-centered workplace safety intervention. Future empirical research should validate the framework across diverse industrial environments and determine whether improved violation detection and corrective-action timeliness translate into sustained reductions in hazardous exposure and preventable eye and face injuries.

items.title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
items.abstract: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.

items.title: From AI Dialogue to Open Access: Making a Scholar's Foundational Works Accessible
items.abstract: This reflective case study documents how sustained collaboration with ChatGPT helped Jean-Pol Martin make his doctoral dissertation (1985) and habilitation thesis (1994) openly accessible. According to Martin’s retrospective account, AI dialogue introduced publication possibilities he had not previously considered and supported the organization of a process involving digitization, publisher permission, legal assistance and coordination with the University Library of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt. Over approximately two months, at a reported cost of EUR 400, both foundational works were made available through Zenodo and the university’s publication server, KU.edoc. The dissertation’s two microfiche supplements were also digitized and published. Inclusion of the digital editions in the library catalogue was pending at the reporting cut-off. The paper examines the complementary contributions of AI assistance, human initiative and institutional infrastructure. Its contribution to the ongoing exploration of Martin’s human-AI model is a documented implementation process whose outputs extend beyond jointly generated text: publicly accessible primary sources. The study distinguishes demonstrated accessibility from potential future effects on discovery, scholarly reception and citation impact. It also addresses limitations concerning retrospective testimony, machine readability and long-term preservation. Prepared with ChatGPT assistance; presented as a reflective working paper, not as peer-reviewed research.

items.title: From Fields Medalists' Concerns to Hidden Capture: A Tale of Two Simulated Worlds of Human Cognition
items.abstract: Hidden capture is a loss of skill that the people losing it do not notice, combined with a dependence that does not reverse when the pressure behind it eases. The Correction Freeze Problem predicts this pattern, but testing it on human thinking would take decades of data that do not yet exist for generative AI. We therefore built a computer simulation of a population, calibrated to what can be measured today, and followed it across generations in two worlds that share the same machines. In World M, AI mostly replaces people’s own practice, and each generation learns what normal ability looks like from the one before. In World N, AI mostly supports practice, and each generation’s sense of normal ability is anchored in direct experience, including time in nature. The model reproduces today’s rise of AI-written text in student work, the share of people who check AI output, and how loosely people’s opinions of their own thinking track tested performance. The simulations show what a captured world would be like from the inside. Delegation stays modest for a while and then sweeps through most of the population within a few years, because each person who hands over their thinking makes it more normal for everyone else. Skill then drains away without being felt. In World M, the average person’s unaided ability fell to about the bottom tenth of the population before AI, yet people registered only a small part of that loss, about a quarter even a century later, because their machine-assisted work looked as good as ever and everyone around them had declined too. The habit of checking disappeared first: at full delegation, only two people in a hundred still compared the machine’s answers with their own judgment, and when the machine’s error rate was quietly doubled, about one in a hundred noticed within five years. In an illustrative century, easing the pressure after a generation of heavy delegation restored only World N; the other two worlds were still captured half a century later. Staying out of the trap proved far easier than climbing out of it. These findings are conditional projections, not forecasts. Across 2,176 sensitivity runs, the unseen loss appeared every time, and its size depended mainly on two things societies can influence now: whether AI replaces or supports people’s own practice, and whether each generation anchors its sense of competence in direct experience. Whether capture can be undone depended on one quantity not yet measured, how much an individual’s reliance on AI changes from year to year; if reliance churns, capture becomes reversible, though it stays hidden. Several earlier results weakened as the model was corrected, and the main pre-specified test of a final extension came back negative; both are reported.

items.title: From psychological needs to knowledge practices: individual inquiry and shared learning in generative AI-supported vocational education
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.

items.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
items.abstract: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.
